entities.description: A value domain describes the allowed values, independently of the shape of a collection. The imaginary unit i satisfies i squared equals minus one. Category labels identify classes rather than numerical magnitudes; storing a category as an integer code does not make it quantitative. A Boolean value is a logical truth value, true or false. Booleans can also be treated as a special two-category domain, but their logical meaning is distinct. Numeric, categorical and Boolean entries can be collected in vectors or rectangular arrays; the preceding real-valued matrix was only one example. These are illustrative value domains, not an exhaustive or disjoint taxonomy.

entities.description:
A response model describes how an observed signal relates to explanatory quantities under stated conditions. In the additive UV/Vis model ([[ref:ex:l1-sm-uvvis-model]]), the systematic concentration-dependent contribution and the remaining contribution together describe the measured response. The attached symbol legend states the role and unit of every term.

The general form in [[ref:ex:l1-sm-general-model]] makes the same organization available for other analytical relationships. Choosing the systematic function is a scientific modelling decision: a straight-line response can be suitable over one concentration range, while curvature can become relevant over another. The remaining term describes departures at the model's chosen level of detail. Its interpretation depends on the recorded conditions and on what the function already represents.

The function families in [[ref:ex:l1-sm-families]] provide several possible shapes for that systematic relationship. Selection draws on chemical mechanism, experimental design and the pattern of observations. After fitting, the departures help assess whether the chosen shape adequately describes the conditions of use. This creates a cycle: formulate a relationship, compare it with observations, and refine its scope or structure.
entities.label: Separate the systematic response from remaining variation

entities.description:
A variable identifies a property that can take different values. An observation records a value of that property for a specified object or occasion. In a calibration, concentration and absorbance are different variables; a prepared standard has a concentration, and an instrument reading supplies an observed absorbance. Their units and roles make the relationship interpretable.

The dilution series in [[ref:ex:l1-sm-flasks]] gives this distinction a chemical setting. Preparing standards establishes a planned set of concentrations. Measuring them adds instrument responses. The table in [[ref:ex:l1-sm-calibration-table]] keeps the controlled concentrations, observed responses and observation identities connected. These roles determine which quantity a calibration model will use to explain or predict another quantity.

The response plot in [[ref:ex:l1-sm-calibration-chart]] then displays the relationship between the two numerical variables. Reading the axes is the first interpretation step: each point represents an observation with a concentration coordinate and an absorbance coordinate. A model can summarize the pattern while repeated readings reveal how much response varies at a given concentration.
entities.label: Give every observed value a variable, unit and role

entities.description:
The shape of a recorded value describes its organization. A scalar is one value, a vector is an ordered collection, and a matrix arranges values along two indices. The examples in [[ref:ex:l1-sm-scalar]], [[ref:ex:l1-sm-vector]] and [[ref:ex:l1-sm-matrix]] connect these shapes with the authored notation. Index meanings determine what a position in the collection represents, such as an observation or a measured channel.

Value type answers a different question: which distinctions and operations are meaningful? Numerical values support quantitative operations in their defined scale and units ([[ref:ex:l1-sm-number]]). Categories identify classes ([[ref:ex:l1-sm-category]]). Boolean values record whether a specified statement holds ([[ref:ex:l1-sm-boolean]]). Numerical storage codes for categories retain their meaning through the category labels and coding convention.

Before analysis, therefore, document both organization and meaning: observation identity, variable name, unit, value type and index convention. These choices make later summaries interpretable and reproducible. They also prepare the next question: which summary of a set of values corresponds to the chemical process and decision under study?
entities.label: Choose a data representation that preserves meaning

entities.description:
A lake study adds a second level of organization. A sampling site identifies where water was collected, while a repeated reading identifies a measurement of that collected material. The map in [[ref:ex:l1-sm-sites]] establishes the spatial setting; the observation table in [[ref:ex:l1-sm-site-table]] retains the site and replicate grouping.

The grouped plot in [[ref:ex:l1-sm-site-chart]] lets us compare variation within sites with differences between sites. Repeated instrument readings characterize the part of the procedure that was repeated. Collecting independent water samples additionally represents sampling variation. A design that repeats both stages allows their contributions to be studied separately.

This reasoning also applies inside an instrument. The variation-source diagram in [[ref:ex:l1-sm-variation]] organizes contributions along the UV/Vis measurement process. Preparation, measurement conditions and electronics can each affect the response. Identifying those stages helps us choose what to hold stable, what to vary deliberately and what to record as context for interpretation.
entities.label: The repeated unit determines which variation is observed

entities.description: Standard deviation is the non-negative square root of a variance. This does not mean that every purely descriptive standard deviation of sample data must use n − 1, and taking the square root does not automatically yield an unbiased estimator of population standard deviation.

|> Calibration standards: concentrations are assigned; absorbance is measured.

We observe how values differ under the study's sampling and measurement conditions. A variable's role depends on the design.
|> Lake samples: concentration may vary with the environment, sampling and measurement.

entries.description: Aᵢ is the observed absorbance of measurement i. Absorbance is dimensionless; i identifies the observation. The equals sign states the model decomposition, and + adds contributions on the absorbance scale.

f(cᵢ) is the modelled absorbance for concentration cᵢ of observation i. cᵢ uses the concentration unit declared for the calibration; f maps that concentration to dimensionless absorbance. Parentheses denote function evaluation.

εᵢ is the residual: observed absorbance minus modelled absorbance for observation i, on the same dimensionless absorbance scale. Its distribution and expectation require additional modelling assumptions.

descriptions.value: Course orientation, lecturer context, learning workflow, materials and introduction activities.
Basic statistical measures, location and dispersion, distributions and statistical moments.

Theoretical distributions: density, cumulative probability and quantiles; normal, lognormal, chi-square, Student-t and F models. Follow-up topics: hypothesis testing, t- and F-tests, distribution tests, ANOVA, multivariate similarity, clustering and component analysis.
Linear and non-linear regression, model diagnostics and machine-learning methods for prediction and classification.
Normalization, smoothing and denoising with convolution, Savitzky-Golay methods, Fourier filtering and wavelet analysis.
Measurement uncertainty, uncertainty propagation, errors and bias, outliers, bootstrap methods and classification-error concepts.
Downhill-simplex optimization and design of experiments including factorial, fractional and response-surface designs.

sections.body:
A variable identifies a property that can take different values. An observation records a value of that property for a specified object or occasion. In a calibration, concentration and absorbance are different variables; a prepared standard has a concentration, and an instrument reading supplies an observed absorbance. Their units and roles make the relationship interpretable.

The dilution series in [[ref:ex:l1-sm-flasks]] gives this distinction a chemical setting. Preparing standards establishes a planned set of concentrations. Measuring them adds instrument responses. The table in [[ref:ex:l1-sm-calibration-table]] keeps the controlled concentrations, observed responses and observation identities connected. These roles determine which quantity a calibration model will use to explain or predict another quantity.

The response plot in [[ref:ex:l1-sm-calibration-chart]] then displays the relationship between the two numerical variables. Reading the axes is the first interpretation step: each point represents an observation with a concentration coordinate and an absorbance coordinate. A model can summarize the pattern while repeated readings reveal how much response varies at a given concentration.

sections.body:
A lake study adds a second level of organization. A sampling site identifies where water was collected, while a repeated reading identifies a measurement of that collected material. The map in [[ref:ex:l1-sm-sites]] establishes the spatial setting; the observation table in [[ref:ex:l1-sm-site-table]] retains the site and replicate grouping.

The grouped plot in [[ref:ex:l1-sm-site-chart]] lets us compare variation within sites with differences between sites. Repeated instrument readings characterize the part of the procedure that was repeated. Collecting independent water samples additionally represents sampling variation. A design that repeats both stages allows their contributions to be studied separately.

This reasoning also applies inside an instrument. The variation-source diagram in [[ref:ex:l1-sm-variation]] organizes contributions along the UV/Vis measurement process. Preparation, measurement conditions and electronics can each affect the response. Identifying those stages helps us choose what to hold stable, what to vary deliberately and what to record as context for interpretation.

sections.body:
A response model describes how an observed signal relates to explanatory quantities under stated conditions. In the additive UV/Vis model ([[ref:ex:l1-sm-uvvis-model]]), the systematic concentration-dependent contribution and the remaining contribution together describe the measured response. The attached symbol legend states the role and unit of every term.

The general form in [[ref:ex:l1-sm-general-model]] makes the same organization available for other analytical relationships. Choosing the systematic function is a scientific modelling decision: a straight-line response can be suitable over one concentration range, while curvature can become relevant over another. The remaining term describes departures at the model's chosen level of detail. Its interpretation depends on the recorded conditions and on what the function already represents.

The function families in [[ref:ex:l1-sm-families]] provide several possible shapes for that systematic relationship. Selection draws on chemical mechanism, experimental design and the pattern of observations. After fitting, the departures help assess whether the chosen shape adequately describes the conditions of use. This creates a cycle: formulate a relationship, compare it with observations, and refine its scope or structure.

sections.body:
The shape of a recorded value describes its organization. A scalar is one value, a vector is an ordered collection, and a matrix arranges values along two indices. The examples in [[ref:ex:l1-sm-scalar]], [[ref:ex:l1-sm-vector]] and [[ref:ex:l1-sm-matrix]] connect these shapes with the authored notation. Index meanings determine what a position in the collection represents, such as an observation or a measured channel.

Value type answers a different question: which distinctions and operations are meaningful? Numerical values support quantitative operations in their defined scale and units ([[ref:ex:l1-sm-number]]). Categories identify classes ([[ref:ex:l1-sm-category]]). Boolean values record whether a specified statement holds ([[ref:ex:l1-sm-boolean]]). Numerical storage codes for categories retain their meaning through the category labels and coding convention.

Before analysis, therefore, document both organization and meaning: observation identity, variable name, unit, value type and index convention. These choices make later summaries interpretable and reproducible. They also prepare the next question: which summary of a set of values corresponds to the chemical process and decision under study?
